title: Score matching, Tweedie and the SDE view

questions.q: What is the score of a density p(x)?
options: The gradient of log p with respect to x
The probability of x
The loss of the network
The noise level at x
questions.answer: The gradient of log p with respect to x
questions.why: s(x) = ∇ₓ log p(x). It needs no normalising constant.

questions.q: By Tweedie's formula, the best denoiser at noise level σ equals
options: x − σ s(x)
x + σ² s(x)
The score alone, scaled by σ²
x / σ
questions.why: E[x_0 | x] = x + σ² ∇log p_σ(x). The lab checks it against four million samples.

questions.q: Why can denoising score matching train on the true score without knowing it?
options: It estimates the score by finite differences
It uses a pretrained classifier
Its loss differs from the explicit loss only by a constant independent of the model
It only works on Gaussian data
questions.answer: Its loss differs from the explicit loss only by a constant independent of the model
questions.why: This is Vincent's identity, and the lab shows the same gap for four very different models.

questions.q: Compared with the probability-flow ODE at the same noise level, the reverse SDE has
options: The same drift and no noise
Half the drift plus noise
Twice the score drift plus fresh noise
No score term at all
questions.answer: Twice the score drift plus fresh noise
questions.why: The reverse SDE uses g²∇log p, the ODE ½g²∇log p, and only the SDE adds dW̄.

questions.q: The ODE and the SDE share
options: The same marginal distribution at every noise level
The same path for each sample
The same random numbers
The same number of model calls per step
questions.answer: The same marginal distribution at every noise level
questions.why: Song et al. 2020 construct the ODE to have the SDE's marginals. Individual paths differ, as the lab's 2.35 RMS difference shows.
